stops.title: The question
stops.text: Every paper so far made each step of the model cheaper. TeaCache asks a different question: do we need to run the transformer at every step at all? In a video diffusion model, neighbouring denoising steps often produce almost the same output. If we can tell which steps are near duplicates, we can reuse the last result instead. No training is needed, and it sits on top of quantization. For the thesis, where one step of LTX-2.3 on a CPU is slow, this could be the biggest win of all.

stops.title: Skip passes, keep steps
stops.text: Here is the whole idea in one picture. The sampler still walks through every step. But the expensive transformer only runs when the input has drifted far enough since the last real computation. On the other steps, a cached result patches the gap. Look at the right side: the decision itself costs one modulation layer and one simple difference measure. That is almost nothing compared with a full pass through dozens of transformer blocks.

stops.title: Why fixed skipping fails
stops.text: So why not just skip every other step? This curve shows how much the output changes between consecutive steps, and it is not flat. It changes fast at the start and the end, and very little in the middle. A fixed pattern is wrong in both directions. It reuses stale outputs where the video is changing quickly, and it still recomputes in the calm middle where several skips in a row would be safe. And there is a catch: the true output change is only known after the model has run.

stops.title: Add up the change
stops.text: That is the problem. Here is the fix. At each step, TeaCache measures how much a cheap input signal changed, and adds that number to a running total. While the total stays below a threshold called delta, the step reuses the cache. When the total crosses delta, the model runs for real and the total resets to zero. That gives this sawtooth. The numbers here are a toy example, but notice the behaviour: long reuse streaks in the quiet middle, and a real computation at almost every step near the end.

stops.title: Cache the residual
stops.text: The second trick is what gets cached. TeaCache does not store the finished output. It stores the residual, the transformer stack's output minus its input. On a skipped step, the sampler has already updated the input, so adding the old residual to this fresh input still moves the video forward. The full noise schedule is preserved. This small detail is why skipping with TeaCache is much gentler than simply deleting steps, as we will see in a moment.

stops.title: Choosing the signal
stops.text: Now, which cheap signal should we watch? These curves are redrawn from the paper, so read the shapes, not the values. The raw noisy input barely changes, so it says nothing. But the noisy input after the timestep embedding has scaled and shifted it, right at the first block, follows the rhythm of the real output change. That modulated input is the indicator. Its raw change does not match the output exactly, so the authors fit a small polynomial once, offline, to rescale it.

stops.title: Caching beats fewer steps
stops.text: Here is a fair test with the same compute budget. Halving Open-Sora from thirty steps to fifteen coarsens the noise schedule, and VBench drops by 1.88 points. TeaCache keeps all thirty sampler steps but skips half of the transformer passes, and loses only 0.34 points. The lesson is simple and useful here: skip model passes, not sampler steps. The frames stay sharp.

stops.title: Does it work?
stops.text: The main results agree. The slow setting of TeaCache is 1.86 times faster on Latte and 1.55 times faster on Open-Sora with no VBench loss, and it beats the rival caching method PAB on both speed and quality. On OpenSora-Plan it reaches 4.41 times. Keep the caveat in mind, though. That big jump comes from a 150 step schedule full of near duplicate steps. A model that already uses few steps, like a distilled LTX checkpoint, will gain less.

stops.title: What the thesis takes from it
stops.text: So what does the thesis take from it? Caching is best treated as its own ablation: quantization alone, caching alone, and both together. It needs no custom kernels, only control flow in the Python denoising loop. The OpenVINO model is split into embedding and modulation, the block stack, and the head, so the loop can read the indicator and cache the residual. The polynomial should be refit on the quantized model, starting with a cautious delta. Finally, VBench shows how to measure whether all these shortcuts still produce good video.
